clue.text: Spoke in no uncertain way to the vehicle that turned sharply

definitions.meaning: to speak each syllable clearly and distinctly
a lorry jointed between cab and trailer, which lets it take tight corners

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both enunciated clearly and jointed, as a lorry with a hinged trailer is.

clue.text: First name of Mrs. Overdone assisting in the bakehouse ?

definitions.text: First name of Mrs. Overdone assisting in the bakehouse ?

parts.words: First name of Mrs. Overdone assisting in the bakehouse ?
parts.note: King Alfred let the cakes burn, so a woman named after him would overdo the baking; Mistress Overdone is in Measure for Measure

explanation.walkthrough: King Alfred famously burnt the cakes; the feminine form of his name suits a woman called Overdone working in a bakehouse. Mistress Overdone is a bawd in Shakespeare's Measure for Measure.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's name, the feminine of the king who let the cakes burn.

clue.text: Cards left on Mr. Bird

definitions.meaning: the stock of cards left after the deal in some games
the claw on a bird of prey's foot

explanation.definitionFit: A term for the undealt stock in cards, and the hooked claw of a bird of prey.

clue.text: Shakespearian firearms may still be legal

definitions.meaning: small cannon fired for salutes, mentioned in Henry IV and Henry VIII
the set of rooms used by barristers, still in legal use

explanation.definitionFit: Old small cannon in Shakespeare, and barristers' offices in the Inns of Court.

clue.text: School not attended by Chaucer's of course

annotationWithheld.clue: School not attended by Chaucer's of course

clue.text: Occasions for Sheffield sporting post-mortems ?

parts.note: Sheffield Wednesday is a football club, so the match is discussed on the following day

explanation.walkthrough: Sheffield Wednesday is an English football club; a post-mortem on its match comes the day after Wednesday.
explanation.definitionFit: The days after Wednesday, when a Wednesday match would be picked over.

clue.text: Plug of tobacco for Eliza's father in extremis

indicators.note: only the extremes of the name are kept, its middle letters dropped

parts.note: Alfred Doolittle is Eliza's father in Shaw's Pygmalion

explanation.surface: Eliza's father, at the end, gets a plug of tobacco.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in extremis' keeps only the ends of DOOLITTLE, Eliza's dustman father in Shaw's Pygmalion: drop the middle OLI to leave DO and TTLE.
explanation.definitionFit: The unburnt plug of tobacco left in the bottom of a pipe bowl.

clue.text: Dignitary returning on a scooter ?

indicators.note: returning means the word for the dignitary is read backwards

parts.note: Dom is a title given to certain church dignitaries and Benedictine monks

explanation.surface: A grandee comes home riding a scooter.
explanation.walkthrough: In the 1960s the Mods were a youth cult famous for riding motor scooters, so a member is someone found on a scooter.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of the sixties youth cult rode Vespas and Lambrettas as their badge.

clue.text: Clement Day needs no such proof

definitions.text: Clement Day needs no such proof

parts.words: Clement Day needs no such proof
parts.note: on a mild day no waterproof coat is needed; Clement reads as a man's name

explanation.walkthrough: Clement looks like a man's name, but means mild: a mild day needs no waterproof, and 'proof' is short for that.
explanation.definitionFit: A rubberised waterproof coat, named after its Scottish inventor.

clue.text: No life on the ocean wave ?

definitions.text: No life on the ocean wave ?

parts.words: No life on the ocean wave ?
parts.note: the salt lake between Israel and Jordan, where nothing can live, plays on the song A Life on the Ocean Wave

explanation.definitionFit: The salt lake on Israel's border is so briny that no fish lives in it.

clue.text: Composer a trifle ornamental if ho reached fifty

indicators.note: ho is an old call to halt, so the word stops when it reaches its final fifty, the Roman L

parts.note: a fal-lal is a showy trifle, a piece of finery

explanation.surface: A composer is mocked as a decorative trifle who might have lived to fifty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ho!' is an old cry of 'stop!': the trinket word halts at its last L, which is fifty in Roman numerals, so that L goes. Manuel de Falla was a Spanish composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Manuel de Falla was the Spanish composer of The Three-Cornered Hat.

clue.text: Hard cases theirs

parts.note: read as the creatures whose bodies are kept in hard shells, not tough characters

explanation.definitionFit: Crabs, lobsters and shrimps form the class of animals with tough jointed shells.

clue.text: Raise by means of handle

parts.note: a handle is slang for a title, so to raise someone is to give them one, making them a peer

explanation.definitionFit: To elevate someone to the peerage gives them a title, slangily a handle to their name.

clue.text: " And near him rode on his ass… Tipsily quaffing " (Keats)

definitions.text: " And near him rode on his ass… Tipsily quaffing " (Keats)

parts.words: " And near him rode on his ass… Tipsily quaffing " (Keats)
parts.note: the missing name in Keats's Endymion is the drunken old companion of Bacchus who rides a donkey

explanation.walkthrough: The gap in the quotation from Keats's Endymion is filled by the fat, tipsy tutor of Bacchus in Greek myth, always shown riding an ass.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth this satyr, foster-father of Dionysus, is pictured drunk astride a donkey.

clue.text: Eden evergreen ?

parts.note: the Latin for the tree of life that grew in Eden, also the name of a conifer

explanation.definitionFit: Latin for tree of life, as in Genesis's garden, and the name of the thuja, an evergreen conifer.

clue.text: What more natural than a sign of affection from Marge?

definitions.text: What more natural than a sign of affection from Marge?

parts.words: What more natural than a sign of affection from Marge?
parts.note: marge is margarine, the dairy spread's rival, and a pat is both a caress and a small pat of spread

explanation.walkthrough: Marge is British slang for margarine; a pat is a light touch of affection and also a small pressed portion of spread.
explanation.definitionFit: A small moulded portion of dairy spread served at table.

clue.text: Wartime hardware-get it ? Jerry can

parts.note: Jerry is slang for a German soldier, who can win this German military decoration, not the fuel can

explanation.walkthrough: Jerry is wartime British slang for a German; a jerrycan is a fuel can, but here the German can get the medal.
explanation.definitionFit: The German military decoration for bravery, made of metal.

clue.text: She has company on the Riviera

definitions.text: She has company on the Riviera

parts.words: She has company on the Riviera
parts.note: a woman's name followed by CO, for company, makes the Riviera principality

explanation.walkthrough: Add CO (company) to this girl's name and you get the tiny principality on the French Riviera.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl's name which, with CO added, spells the principality beside Nice.

clue.text: The Spanish Gypsy as a musical

definitions.text: The Spanish Gypsy as a musical

parts.words: The Spanish Gypsy as a musical
parts.note: the title heroine of Vincent Wallace's opera is a Gypsy singer in Madrid

explanation.definitionFit: The 1845 opera by William Vincent Wallace about a Gypsy street singer in Madrid.

clue.text: Foreign seaboard refuge of the fleeced

definitions.meaning: French for coast, as in the Riviera's name
a shelter for sheep or doves

explanation.definitionFit: French for coast, and an English word for a shelter for sheep.

clue.text: It tends to eclipse the half-moon

definitions.text: It tends to eclipse the half-moon

parts.words: It tends to eclipse the half-moon
parts.note: the half-moon is the pale crescent at the base of a fingernail, which a fold of skin can cover

explanation.walkthrough: The half-moon is the lunula, the pale crescent at a fingernail's base, which the fold of skin can grow over.
explanation.definitionFit: The skin fold at the base of a nail that overlaps the pale lunula.

clue.text: So, tea, chums — for which the things are under your noses

definitions.text: the things are under your noses

indicators.note: the three words are to be rearranged into what follows, the letters giving the things described

explanation.surface: Inviting friends to tea, someone points out what is right under their noses.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a friendly invitation; 'for which' is the only signal that the first three words are to be rearranged into what follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Facial hair grown on the upper lip sits directly below the nose.

clue.text: Look, ripping playthings !

parts.note: look means see
ripping tools are saws, as in a ripsaw

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims at some splendid toys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ripping' looks like old slang for splendid, but stands for the tools that rip.
explanation.definitionFit: Playground planks balanced on a pivot that children ride up and down.

clue.text: Made investigation for sleeping accommodation

parts.note: pro is Latin for for, as in pros and cons
a bed is somewhere to sleep

explanation.surface: Someone looked into a place to sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: To have explored or examined something closely.

clue.text: Theobald and Richard begin to collaborate concerning public spectacles

parts.note: the name begins THEO, its usual short form
the name begins RIC, its usual short form

explanation.surface: Two men start working together on a book about public shows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'begin' asks for the opening of each name, Theo and Ric, which 'collaborate' by joining. The word describes the ancient Athenian fund for public spectacles.
explanation.definitionFit: An old adjective for things relating to theatrical shows, as the Athenian fund paying citizens' entry to festivals.

clue.text: Sort of tripe he produces, if you please !

indicators.note: sort is taken as a verb, to sort or rearrange the letters given

explanation.surface: A man produces some kind of offal and politely offers it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of' tells you to rearrange TRIPE and HE.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic contraction of I pray thee, used as a polite request.

clue.text: Dough for adornment

definitions.meaning: flour and water mixed into a soft mass
imitation gems of glass for jewellery

explanation.definitionFit: A soft mix of flour and water, and glass used for fake jewels.

clue.text: I say ! ship's empty

parts.note: a ship's body is its hull
empty is nothing, zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A sailor calls out that the vessel is empty.
explanation.definitionFit: A greeting or exclamation of surprise, like hello.

clue.text: Pirated editions ?

parts.note: books that have been copied, not exercise books for handwriting practice

explanation.definitionFit: Exercise books with model handwriting; read literally, books that are copies.

clue.text: Everything and nothing has a Scots burgh

parts.note: everything means all
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A Scottish town is said to have everything and nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: Alloa is a small town on the River Forth in Scotland, famous for brewing.
explanation.definitionFit: Alloa is a town in Clackmannanshire on the north bank of the Forth.

clue.text: Or stir and drink

parts.note: the word pairs with drink in the phrase for taking food and drink, and stirred gives a hot drink

explanation.walkthrough: The clue offers two routes: the word goes with 'drink' in the familiar phrase for consuming, or its letters, stirred, make a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: To consume food, the usual partner of drinking.

clue.text: Hardy remedies do these employ ?

parts.note: Thomas Hardy's first novel was Desperate Remedies, the measures reckless outlaws resort to

explanation.walkthrough: Hardy's first novel is called Desperate Remedies; desperate men, reckless outlaws, are the ones who use such measures.
explanation.definitionFit: Reckless outlaws of the Wild West kind, ready to use desperate means.
